title: Chacra Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Chacra wells have a median depth of 85 feet. Review local yields, water levels, drillers, risks, and estimated well costs.
h1: What Chacra Well Records Tell You Before You Buy
intro_html:
Buying land near Chacra means evaluating the well record along with the house, road, septic system, and building site. Permit data within five miles shows generally shallow wells, strong reported yields, and a water level that is often close to the surface. The records are useful for planning, but they are not a guarantee for an unbuilt lot.

Of 486 wells in the Colorado Division of Water Resources records, 216 are recorded as constructed. Only 274 report total depth, 95 report pump yield, and 35 report static water level. That uneven reporting matters: use the local pattern to budget and ask questions, then confirm the specific parcel with a driller and the state permit file.

sections.heading: Chacra well depths are usually shallow
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Chacra is 85 feet, with the middle half between 56 and 160 feet. That gives a driller a reasonable starting range, but not a firm bid. A deeper result is still possible: the 90th percentile is 232 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 2,203 feet.

The depth mix is favorable for shallow drilling. Fifty-eight percent of reported wells are under 100 feet, while 36% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Five percent are between 300 and 600 feet, and none are recorded above 600 feet in that mix. Local ground includes mixed sedimentary and alluvial material, while most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. Rock changes, alluvial thickness, casing, and grout requirements can move a final price well beyond a simple depth calculation.

sections.heading: Reported Chacra yields are generally useful
sections.html:
Among the 95 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 15 gallons per minute, and the middle half ranges from 12 to 15 gallons per minute. Sixty-nine percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. Twenty-six percent fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 4% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute.

Those figures suggest that a typical completed well may support ordinary household use, but yield is not the same as guaranteed daily supply. Pump testing, storage capacity, water pressure equipment, and the legal use allowed by the permit all matter. A buyer should request the well construction and pump records rather than relying only on a neighboring result.

sections.heading: Water levels near Chacra and what the record shows
sections.html:
The median static water level is 20 feet below ground, with the middle half between 12 and 66 feet. That is a relatively accessible water level for drilling and pump installation, but it also means construction details deserve attention. Casing and grout need to protect the borehole from surface water, especially where drainage, irrigation, or septic systems are nearby.

The available record does not provide a water-level series by decade, so it does not establish a dropping or rising long-term water table. Only 35 wells report static water level, a small subset compared with the total permit file. Ask for a recent measurement on the specific property and compare it with nearby wells when the purchase decision depends on pumping depth or seasonal reliability.

sections.heading: Chacra permit history and the drillers on record
sections.html:
Permit activity has been strongest since the late twentieth century. The records show 150 permits from the 1990s, 96 from the 2000s, 40 from the 1980s, 38 from the 2010s, and 33 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. Domestic or household wells make up 56% of the use mix; monitoring accounts for 22%, irrigation 8%, and stock 7%.

Shelton Drilling Corporation, listed with Shelton, Wayne, appears most often with 142 records. Collins Drilling Co, listed with Collins, F. E. “Bodie,” appears on 61. Authorized, listed as Pe, Pg, appears on 25. These records show who has worked in the area, not a quality ranking. Confirm current licensing, insurance, references, and the scope of each written bid before hiring.

sections.heading: What a new Chacra well may cost
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground described for Chacra, the planning rate is $50 to $75 per foot. At the 85-foot median depth, the drilled hole calculates to about $4,200 to $6,400. A finished well, including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, is estimated at about $10,200 to $18,400.

Use those figures as a budgeting range, not a guaranteed contract price. A bid can change with access, casing and grout, hard layers, water-quality requirements, pump depth, electrical distance, and the final well design. Before closing on a lot, ask the driller to separate drilling, casing, development, pump equipment, trenching, electrical work, testing, and permit-related services so you can see what is included.

sections.heading: Chacra risks to check before construction
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main pattern in the reported data, but a good area-wide median cannot rule out a poor hole on one parcel. Fractured-bedrock wells can be unpredictable, and the record includes a wide depth spread. Confirm the permit status, construction report, test yield, static level, pump setting, and water-quality results for the property whenever those documents exist.

Environmental screening also deserves attention. Within about 10 miles, the map shows 79 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 31 historic mine features. There are no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites mapped in that radius. Those map findings do not prove contamination at a particular well, so arrange laboratory testing and check drainage, mine history, fuel storage, and septic locations. A septic system must fit the lot, groundwater conditions, setbacks, and local approval requirements.

sections.heading: A practical plan for a Chacra lot
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado Division of Water Resources permit file and identify the well tied to the parcel, not merely the closest mapped point. Then compare nearby New Castle, Glenwood Springs, No Name, Silt, Cattle Creek, and Carbonate records only as local context; conditions can change across short distances. Have a licensed driller inspect access, proposed house placement, septic space, power routing, and the likely drilling location before you commit.

For an existing home, make the purchase contingent on reviewing the well permit, construction report, pump test, water test, and equipment condition. For vacant land, budget from the 85-foot median but keep room for a deeper result and site work. A written feasibility review can uncover access or septic problems before excavation, when changing the building plan is still practical.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Chacra, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth near Chacra is 85 feet, with the middle half between 56 and 160 feet. Fifty-eight percent are under 100 feet, while 36% are between 100 and 300 feet. The 90th percentile is 232 feet, so a particular parcel can require substantially more drilling than the local median.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Chacra?
faq.a: The local planning rate is $50 to $75 per foot. At the 85-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $4,200 to $6,400. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $10,200 to $18,400. Access, casing, grout, hard layers, and equipment can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Chacra wells produce?
faq.a: Among 95 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 15 gallons per minute and the middle half is 12 to 15 gallons per minute. Sixty-nine percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. These figures describe recorded tests, not a guarantee for a new well, so request a pump test and confirm the permit’s legal use.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Chacra?
faq.a: The area map shows 79 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 31 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites mapped there. That does not determine the quality of an individual well. Test the specific water through a qualified laboratory and review nearby land uses, drainage, mine history, and septic locations.
